source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Chapter III, §19 Winning by Indirect Attack, Example 49

steps.title: Two courses
steps.source: An examination of this position will show that Black's main weakness lies in the exposed position of his King, and in the fact that his Q R has not yet come into the game.

narration.say: Black's weaknesses: the exposed king, and the rook on a8 not yet in play.
If it were Black's move, he might even be better: three pawns to two on the queen side, and the bishop on the long diagonal.
The obvious move, Bc4, might be good enough. But another move upsets Black's position completely.

feedback.Bc4: The obvious move: good enough, after Rad8 and b4. But there is a stronger one.
feedback.*: A knight move, into the centre.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Find the move that wins a pawn.

narration.say: The bishop on c6 is now undefended.

feedback.*: The rook on c1 takes on c6.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Take the bishop.
exercise.wrong: The rook on c1 takes on c6.
exercise.success: 2. Rxc6. Black plays Nb4: nothing better, because White threatened Bc4.

narration.say: Bishop to c4, check. King to h8.
Rook to e6, attacking the queen. Pawn to d3.
Rook takes d3. White is a pawn ahead, with the better position.

steps.title: All the pieces together
steps.source: Once the opportunity is offered, all the pieces are thrown into action "en masse" when necessary; and all the pieces smoothly co-ordinate their action with machine-like precision.

narration.say: These positions show different types of combination, and train the imagination.
Once the opportunity is offered, all the pieces are thrown into action, en masse.
And they co-ordinate with machine-like precision.
